statement: The system shall enable investigators to quickly see what is happening in an outbreak.
The system shall enable investigators to connect cases and exposures.
The system shall enable investigators to act early enough to interrupt transmission.
The system shall provide decision-makers with a reliable operational picture.
The system shall enable decision-makers to prioritize resources.
The system shall enable decision-makers to track response progress.
The system shall support defensible public health decisions.
The system shall reduce missed links between people and events.
The system shall provide faster investigation and reporting turnaround.
The system shall improve coordination across the team.
The system shall protect sensitive information appropriately.

The system shall support public health investigators, disease surveillance staff, and outbreak response coordinators as primary users for entering, linking, and analyzing case and contact information.
The system shall provide fast data entry.
The system shall allow users to track relationships across cases, exposures, specimens, and interventions.
The system shall provide a clear workflow for follow-up and status updates.
The system shall support decision-makers and supervisors with situational awareness, trend review, and reporting.
The system shall provide summarized views and timelines for decision-makers and supervisors.
The system shall ensure that decision-makers and supervisors can trust that the data is current.
The system shall support lab and field partners who may contribute information or receive assignments.
The system shall provide lab and field partners with a secure way to share only the information relevant to their role.
The system shall ensure that each contact, exposure, specimen, and intervention is tied to the correct case or event.
The system shall preserve relationship history when case or event linkages are updated.
If a case is marked urgent or high risk, the system shall surface it immediately for the assigned team and move it into a more active follow-up status.
If key information is missing, the system shall flag the record as incomplete and keep it visible until required fields are filled in or the issue is explicitly deferred.
The system shall send escalation alerts to the assigned investigator or supervisor first.
If no action occurs within the expected timeframe, the system shall escalate alerts to broader response leadership.
The system shall comply with privacy and public health data-sharing rules.
The system shall tightly control access to highly sensitive information by role and jurisdiction.
The system shall keep working during surges.
The system shall remain usable when many cases and contacts are coming in at once.
The system shall remain usable when connectivity is spotty in the field or during emergency response.
The system shall support situations where data is incomplete or changing quickly.
The system shall allow users to create core records needed in the field.
The system shall allow users to view cases or assignments that have already been downloaded to the device.
The system shall queue changes locally so users can continue working without losing data.
The system shall synchronize queued changes automatically when connectivity returns.
The system shall not silently overwrite important data when conflicts occur.
The system shall flag data conflicts for review.
The system shall keep both conflicting versions available for review.
The system shall let a designated user decide which update wins based on timestamps and data quality.
The outbreak management system shall integrate with surveillance systems.
The outbreak management system shall integrate with laboratory reporting systems.
The outbreak management system may integrate with immunization systems if immunization systems are part of the investigation workflow.
The outbreak management system may integrate with vital records systems if vital records systems are part of the investigation workflow.
The outbreak management system shall receive case notifications from partner systems.
The outbreak management system shall receive laboratory results from partner systems.
The outbreak management system shall receive specimen details from partner systems.
The outbreak management system shall receive relevant demographic data from partner systems.
The outbreak management system shall receive relevant jurisdictional data from partner systems.
The outbreak management system shall send investigation status to partner systems.
The outbreak management system shall send case identifiers to partner systems.
The outbreak management system shall send specimen requests to partner systems.
The outbreak management system may send classification updates to partner systems.
The system shall use a combination of strong identifiers and demographic matching for record matching.
The system shall use national or local IDs when they are available.
The system shall use name for matching records.
The system shall use date of birth for matching records.
The system shall use sex for matching records.
The system shall use address for matching records.
The system shall use specimen accession numbers for matching records.
The system shall use event dates for matching records.
The system shall automatically link records when there is a high-confidence exact match on a stable identifier.
The system shall flag records for human review when a match is partial or there are conflicts.
The system shall create a new record when the information is too weak or clearly inconsistent.
The system shall keep a potential duplicate visible for later reconciliation when it creates a new record due to weak or inconsistent information.
The system shall make matching rules configurable by agency.
The system shall maintain a complete audit trail for any action that changes a record or a case decision.
The audit trail shall include creates, edits, deletes, status changes, linkage changes, approvals, and exports.
The audit trail shall record who performed each logged action.
The audit trail shall record when each logged action occurred.
The audit trail shall record what changed for each logged action.
The audit trail should ideally include before-and-after values so that the investigation history can be reconstructed.
The logs shall be detailed enough to support compliance review and internal review of decisions.
Investigators and administrators shall be able to review the audit trail long after the outbreak is active.
Access to the audit trail shall be controlled.
The system shall support outbreak investigation.
The system shall support monitoring.
The system shall support analysis.
The system shall support reporting.
The system shall be flexible enough to handle related public health events.
The system shall keep sensitive information protected.
The system shall support the workflows of investigators who use it during outbreaks.
The system shall support the workflows of program managers who use it during outbreaks.
The system shall support reporting needs.
The system shall satisfy data protection requirements.
The current process is fragmented.
Teams often work out of spreadsheets.
Teams often work out of email.
Teams often work out of shared drives.
Teams sometimes work out of separate surveillance systems or case management systems.
Linking cases, contacts, exposures, and specimens happens manually.
Reporting is assembled by hand.
Hand-assembled reporting takes time.
Hand-assembled reporting makes it harder to keep information consistent when the situation is changing quickly.
The system shall reduce manual work required to stitch information together.
The system shall make it easier to see relationships between people, places, events, and lab results in one place.
The system shall provide faster situational awareness through dashboards or summaries.
The system shall provide better role-based access control so that sensitive investigation details are visible only to the right people.
The system shall provide strong search and filtering capabilities.
The system shall enable investigators to find records quickly during a fast-moving event.
The system shall track interventions and follow-up actions over time.
The system shall maintain audit history showing who changed what and when.
The system shall support import and export capabilities.
The system shall support sharing data with other systems or partners.
Investigators and supervisors need timely reminders when a follow-up is due.
The system should provide secure messaging to coordinate sensitive details without relying on email.
Some kind of in-system notification or alerting should be in scope.
For the first release, the system shall prioritize linked management of the core entities.
For the first release, the system shall prioritize role-based access control.
For the first release, the system shall prioritize search and filtering.
After the first release, the system shall include dashboards.
After the first release, the system shall include follow-up tracking.
After the first release, the system shall include audit history.
If the system is phased in further, it shall include notifications.
If the system is phased in further, it shall include secure messaging.
The system shall allow investigators to create and maintain a single view of how a case connects to contacts, exposures, specimens, and interventions instead of treating each as separate records.
The system shall allow users to add relationships as they are discovered.
The system shall allow users to update relationships over time.
The system shall allow users to see the chain of evidence or activity that supports the investigation.
The system shall help users identify when two records may actually belong to the same real-world person or event so that duplication can be avoided.
The system shall support routine outbreak investigations.
The system shall support suspected bioterrorism incidents.
The system shall support foodborne illness clusters.
The system shall support hospital-associated outbreaks.
The system shall support other unusual health incidents that require fast coordination.
The system shall support case finding.
The system shall support contact tracing.
The system shall support monitoring exposed people.
The system shall support tracking specimens and lab results.
The system shall support documenting interventions while the situation is still evolving.
The system shall support long-running monitoring after the initial response.

The outbreak response typically involves epidemiologists, disease investigators, contact tracers, laboratorians, and public health managers, with clinicians and local health partners sometimes involved as well.
Early in an outbreak, investigators are focused on identifying cases, exposures, and contacts.
Early in an outbreak, laboratories help confirm what is happening.
Early in an outbreak, managers oversee priorities, reporting, and resource allocation.
As the outbreak unfolds, contact tracers and monitors take on more follow-up.
As the outbreak unfolds, investigators keep refining the case picture.
As the outbreak unfolds, managers watch the overall status and response actions.
The system shall work well in a fast-moving environment where information is incomplete at first and keeps changing.
The system shall support users starting with a suspected event.
The system shall support users building linked cases and contacts over time.
The system shall support users updating exposure details as new facts come in.
The system shall support users updating specimen details as new facts come in.
The system shall support users updating intervention details as new facts come in.
The system shall support longer follow-up after the initial surge.
The system shall support ongoing checks for some contacts or monitored cases.
The system shall support investigations that remain open for weeks or longer.
The system shall support whatever jurisdiction the public health program is operating in.
The system shall initially support the state-level program.
The system shall potentially support local health departments that connect into the state-level program.
The system shall cover investigation and response activities that the relevant teams are responsible for within their legal authority.
The system shall support coordination across jurisdictions when an outbreak crosses boundaries.
The system shall follow the public health program’s case definitions and investigation protocols.
Case definitions and investigation protocols may vary by disease and jurisdiction.
The system shall open a case when there is a report or signal that meets the threshold for review.
The system shall escalate a case when evidence suggests confirmed risk or wider exposure.
The system shall close a case when the person is no longer under follow-up or the investigation is resolved according to program policy.
The system shall use the program’s written procedures and any applicable legal requirements to determine the exact policy thresholds.
The system shall support intake from electronic lab reports.
The system shall support intake from case reports from clinicians or hospitals.
The system shall support intake from referrals from local health departments.
The system shall support intake from manual reports by phone.
The system shall support intake from email.
The system shall support intake from other urgent notification channels.
The system shall help electronic feeds support higher volume and faster processing.
The system shall require manual channels to be triaged immediately when they may involve a time-sensitive or high-risk situation.
The system shall capture all intake sources in a consistent way.
The system shall help investigators decide quickly what needs action first.
The system shall preserve the core public health workflow.
The system shall support staff reviewing a signal.
The system shall support assigning investigation ownership.
The system shall support documenting case details and contact details.
The system shall support recording actions taken.
The system shall reduce manual re-entry.
The system shall reduce disconnected tracking.
The system shall eliminate reliance on spreadsheets for tracking.
The system shall eliminate reliance on emails for tracking.
The system shall eliminate reliance on separate notes for tracking.
The system shall make linking entities more centralized and consistent.
The system shall make updating statuses more centralized and consistent.
The system shall make producing reports more centralized and consistent.
The system shall not force staff to change the basic investigative process they already follow.
The system shall migrate enough historical data to keep active and recently closed investigations usable.
For older outbreaks, the system shall migrate summary data at minimum.
Changes shall be managed in a controlled way.
The system shall use planned releases rather than frequent surprise updates.
Enhancements shall be tested with public health users before they go live.
Urgent changes shall have a clear approval path and rollback capability if needed.
The system shall maintain a stable core workflow so routine updates do not force staff to relearn case management during an outbreak.
The system shall be deployed in a pilot phase first.
The system shall be rolled out in stages by region or program unit rather than being turned on for everyone at once.
The staged rollout preference is especially applicable when data migration and integrations are involved.
The rollout approach shall allow close user support and problem correction before statewide or cross-jurisdiction use.
Day-to-day support should be handled by the program’s application support team or public health IT operations.
The vendor or implementation partner should handle deeper technical fixes, upgrades, and defects that the internal team cannot resolve.
There should be a clear escalation path for critical issues.
The rollout should include a clean handoff.
The handoff should include training, support documentation, and named contacts for urgent production problems.
The system shall support field work and local health settings where connectivity can be unreliable.
The system shall allow investigators to access recent records when connectivity is unavailable.
The system shall support lifecycle terms including reopened and merged.
The system shall support reclassifying a record when new information changes what it represents.
The system shall allow staff to see both the current status and the prior history of a record.
The system shall preserve the audit trail explaining why a record changed.
The system shall normalize lifecycle labels across programs if labels are not standardized.
Urgent notifications such as phone calls or direct alerts shall be triaged immediately.
Possible cluster reports shall receive immediate triage when urgent notifications suggest a possible cluster.
Death-related notifications shall receive immediate triage when urgent notifications indicate death.
Notifications about other high-risk events shall receive immediate triage when urgent notifications indicate other high-risk events.
Electronic reports may be placed in the normal intake queue.
Electronic reports shall be reviewed within a defined timeframe so that they do not remain unprocessed.
Email and informal notifications may require extra validation because they can arrive incomplete.
The system shall flag incomplete email and informal notifications for follow-up.
The intake channel list shall remain tentative for now.
The system shall allow batch imports as a possible intake source.
The system shall allow feeds from other public health systems as a possible intake source.
The system shall leave room for additional intake sources without forcing everything into a fixed list too early.
The system shall convert full-detail records for active cases and recently closed investigations at go-live.
The system should convert full-detail historical records far enough back to support continuity and reporting for the current outbreak cycle or a defined retention window.
The system shall bring older purely archival records over in a lighter form.
The system shall allow older archival records to be indexed so staff can find them without requiring every detail in the new system.
The system shall apply special handling to legacy investigations that are still referenced often, even if they are older than the normal cutoff.
Staff shall be able to see who made a status change.
Staff shall be able to see when a status change happened.
Staff shall be able to see a short reason or note explaining why a status change was made.
The system shall preserve the chain of events for merged or reclassified records so investigators can understand the decision later.
The record history should not be hidden.
The system may summarize record history for everyday users while keeping the full history available to authorized staff.
The system shall support mapping local labels to a common internal set for reporting and cross-program tracking.
The mapping of local labels to a common internal set shall be configurable.
The system shall treat lab reports, case reports, and referrals as related but distinct source types.
The system shall allow multiple sources to be attached to the same investigation without losing the original details.
Urgent manual notifications shall be surfaced first for triage.
Lab reports and clinician or hospital reports shall usually become part of the standard case build-out.
When the same investigation has more than one source, staff shall be able to see which source arrived first and which sources confirmed or supplemented the record.
Batch imports should be handled cautiously.
Batch imports should be allowed to create new investigations when the match is clear.
Ambiguous batch import records should go into a review queue rather than being processed automatically.
Conflicting batch import records should go into a review queue rather than being processed automatically.
Duplicate batch import records should go into a review queue rather than being processed automatically.
For updates from other systems, the system should flag differences and let authorized staff decide which version to keep when there is any uncertainty.
By default, the system shall capture the intake and not drop it.
The system shall label the intake as an unclassified or other intake source.
The system shall route the intake to a general review queue.
The system shall allow staff to decide whether the intake belongs in an existing investigation or requires a new investigation.
The system shall allow the intake to be escalated if it is sensitive or urgent, even before the source is fully categorized.
The system shall block the automatic update when an imported or externally sourced record partially matches an existing investigation but conflicts on key fields.
The system shall preserve both versions of the record for review when such a conflict occurs.
The system shall show the conflicting fields side by side.
The system shall indicate which source is considered more authoritative when an authoritative source has been defined.
The system shall let staff decide whether to merge the records, keep both as history, or reject the incoming change.
The system may allow a preference rule when the conflict is minor and clearly one-sided.
The system shall determine responsibility shifts using configurable workflow rules rather than hardcoded timing.
Responsibility shall shift immediately only when there is no active urgent work that would be disrupted.
An urgent change shall take effect quickly.
Investigators shall be able to draft notes and queue certain updates while offline.
Linked people, contacts, exposures, and actions shall be editable separately if they belong to different parts of the investigation.
If a linked record is used in multiple active workflows, the system shall control edits carefully to prevent one team from accidentally overwriting information another team still depends on.
The system shall lock a shared record or require supervisor approval when a change affects case status.
The system shall require approval when a shared record is already being edited by another user.
The system shall require approval when a user is trying to change restricted sensitive data.
The system shall allow a time-critical containment update to bypass the lock.
Routine data entry and common lookups should stay very fast, ideally within one to two seconds.
If an operation takes longer than expected, the system should show a clear progress indicator.
If an operation exceeds a reasonable threshold, the system should fail gracefully.

The system shall time out an operation based on the kind of action if it is still running after the progress indicator has been displayed for a while, but it shall not time out so quickly that normal outbreak work is interrupted.
The system shall preserve whatever the user has already typed or selected on the screen when an operation fails or times out.

The system shall allow the user to keep working in other parts of the system while the failed action is retried, provided that nothing has already been reserved or locked in a way that would make this unsafe.
The system shall determine timeout duration based on the criticality and frequency of the action.
The timeout window should be based on how often the action is used.
Anything already committed to the database shall not be rolled back because a later save timed out.
If the underlying record was already submitted or linked by someone else, the system shall clear or flag any conflicting edits so the user must review them before resubmitting.
The system shall treat sensitive or system-generated fields differently from ordinary user-entered fields.
Anything authoritative about identity should be reloaded from the persisted record after a save timeout retry.
The system should reload case status from the persisted record after a save timeout retry.
Fields in this category should not remain tied to the in-progress entry unless they are deliberately staged changes that have not been committed yet.
The user must explicitly confirm deliberately staged changes before they replace the saved value.
The system shall show the user exactly what needs review before any pending edits are applied.
The system shall allow purely local notes or draft comments to remain unchanged.
The system shall highlight edits to shared fields for reconciliation, including demographics, status, relationships, exposures, and specimen details.
Local notes should stay intact.
Shared field edits should be flagged for review.
Intervention narrative fields such as free-text rationale or implementation comments should be treated like notes when they are descriptive and do not drive workflow.
Changes to intervention status should be handled as shared data and reconciled before acceptance.
Changes to intervention dates should be handled as shared data and reconciled before acceptance.
Changes to the assigned person should be handled as shared data and reconciled before acceptance.
Changes to the completion result should be handled as shared data and reconciled before acceptance.
Anything that changes the operational picture in a meaningful way should update immediately.
Updates should be immediate when they affect case status.
Updates should be immediate when they affect contact tracing.
Updates should be immediate when they affect an active investigation queue.
If new lab results arrive or a record changes state in a way that someone needs to act on, the dashboard should refresh right away or at least prompt a near-real-time update.
Slower batch refresh is acceptable for summary trends.
Slower batch refresh is acceptable for counts.
Slower batch refresh is acceptable for historical reporting views where a few minutes of delay will not affect decisions.
The system shall react immediately to status changes that affect triage or assignment.
The system shall react immediately to new exposures that create a new follow-up action.
The system shall react immediately to any item moving into or out of an active queue.
The system shall not wait for the next batch cycle for changes that can alter what an investigator does next.
The system may defer minor edits until the next refresh.
The system may defer metadata tweaks until the next refresh.
The system may defer background updates that do not change workload or risk until the next refresh.
The dashboard shall update immediately for a newly opened case.
The dashboard shall update immediately for a reassigned owner.
The dashboard shall update immediately for a stage change.
The dashboard shall update immediately for any change that opens or closes a case.
Less operational changes, such as edits to notes or noncritical demographics, shall wait until the next batch refresh unless they are tied to an urgent workflow.
During an active incident, the system shall provide very high availability.
During an active incident, the system shall be effectively always on.
The system shall be reliable enough that investigators can depend on it throughout the operational period.
The system shall avoid maintenance or downtime during peak response if at all possible.
If continuous availability cannot be guaranteed, the system shall have a clearly defined fallback and notice process.
The system shall support users who rely on it in real time.
If an incident is still active, planned maintenance should generally be deferred until the operational risk is lower.
If planned maintenance is performed during an active incident, it should be done in a way that does not interrupt investigator access.
If downtime is unavoidable, users should receive advance notice.
If downtime is unavoidable, the system should provide a clear fallback method for capturing critical updates so work is not lost.
The system should remain available whenever possible and should only be taken down when there is a strong reason and a communicated workaround.
Staff shall be able to capture new cases during downtime or recovery scenarios.
Staff shall be able to capture contacts during downtime or recovery scenarios.
Staff shall be able to capture exposures during downtime or recovery scenarios.
Staff shall be able to capture critical actions during downtime or recovery scenarios.
The system shall support temporary offline logging or a paper/emergency form for capturing information during downtime.
The system shall provide a clean handoff process for entering downtime data back into the system later.
The handoff process shall preserve timestamps when downtime data is entered back into the system.
The handoff process shall preserve ownership when downtime data is entered back into the system.
The handoff process shall preserve links between records when downtime data is entered back into the system.
During system recovery, users shall have read-only access to existing case details.
Before an incident starts, the core case workflow, contact workflow, exposure workflow, and reporting workflow shall be proven and ready.
Before an incident starts, access controls and backup procedures shall be in place.
During an incident, the system or team shall prioritize stability.
During an incident, the system or team shall provide quick updates.
During an incident, the system or team shall provide visibility into active work.
Immediately after an incident, the system or team shall reconcile any offline entries.
Immediately after an incident, the system or team shall validate the data.
Immediately after an incident, the system or team shall perform a quick status review to ensure nothing was missed.
Offline records shall not be re-dated to the time of entry unless this is explicitly noted.
Each paper or offline record shall include a unique local identifier or reference so it can be matched back during reconciliation.
Staff shall be able to quickly identify who is connected to the event.
Staff shall be able to track the spread and scope of the event.
Staff shall be able to act on findings without losing important details.
The system shall keep cases linked together in a reliable way.
The system shall keep contacts linked together in a reliable way.
The system shall keep exposures linked together in a reliable way.
The system shall keep interventions linked together in a reliable way.
The system shall support timely containment decisions.
The system shall help the team turn incoming information into coordinated action fast enough to stop further spread.
Releases during an active investigation shall be tightly controlled and performed only when there is a strong operational reason.
Release timing should avoid peak response periods when possible.
Users shall receive advance notice before a release goes out.
The system shall include a quick validation step with a small trusted group before a release goes broadly live.
A rollback plan shall be ready in case an update causes confusion or breaks a workflow.
During an incident, staff shall not be forced to relearn the workflow on the fly.
The deployment approach shall allow exceptions to the normal pilot-first rollout order.
A jurisdiction with a hard dependency on a legacy system shall be deployed using a different sequence or be held back until the dependency is ready.
A jurisdiction with a complex data migration shall be deployed using a different sequence or be held back until the migration is ready.
A jurisdiction with an integration that must be live from day one shall be deployed using a different sequence or be held back until the integration is ready.
Programs with heavier confidentiality or reporting requirements shall receive extra validation before going live.
The system shall treat a release as a no-go if the change would risk slowing down active case finding or contact tracing.
The system shall treat a release as a no-go while the team is still in rapid intake mode.
The system shall treat a release as a no-go while the team is still in triage mode.
The system shall treat a release as a no-go while the team is still in urgent intervention mode.
The system shall allow a release to proceed if the release is absolutely critical.
The system shall allow a release to proceed if staff can absorb a brief interruption and there is a rollback path.
The release guidance should remain tentative for now rather than a firm rule.
The system should avoid peak response periods.
The guidance should not be made a firm rule across every situation until enough conditions have been defined.
The system shall allow an update to proceed during a rapid-response phase if the update fixes a severe security issue.
The system shall allow an update to proceed during a rapid-response phase if the update fixes a data integrity problem.
The system shall allow an update to proceed during a rapid-response phase if the update fixes a system defect that is actively preventing staff from recording or seeing critical outbreak information.
The system shall allow an update to proceed when the update would otherwise leave staff blind to cases, contacts, or exposures.
The system shall allow an update to proceed when the update would create a serious privacy risk.
The system shall allow an urgent update to proceed during an active investigation if the interruption is short and controlled and the update prevents a much bigger operational or safety problem.
The system shall allow an urgent update to proceed when the risk of waiting is worse than the temporary workflow disruption.
Staff shall be informed before an urgent update proceeds.
The outage window for an urgent update shall be very small.
The decision to keep a critical incident within the internal support team should depend on whether the problem can be safely diagnosed and fixed without risking the active investigation.
A critical incident should be escalated when it involves the application code, infrastructure, or an integration that the internal support team does not control.
An issue must be escalated immediately if there is any sign that it could disrupt the investigation or requires vendor code changes or environment changes.
The jurisdiction with the strongest case connection or where the primary public health action is happening should lead coordination.
Only information needed for coordinated response should be shared with partner health departments.
Leadership disputes should be resolved quickly through established public health agreements rather than case by case.
The system shall follow existing public health data standards when sharing case information with partner jurisdictions.
The system shall format shared case information so the receiving side can process it without rework.
The system shall use secure transmission for sharing case information.
The system shall prefer system-to-system exchange when it is available.
Access shall be based on role, jurisdiction, and need to know.
Each team shall be able to edit only the fields or sections it owns for its part of the workflow.
Changes that could affect another team’s work shall be routed through the case lead rather than edited directly.
Changes to core records such as identity, status, exposure linkage, or disposition shall be routed through the case lead rather than edited directly.
The system shall support field work where users may work offline and log the activity later.
The system shall allow the entry time to be used for a specific reason only when that use is explicit and visible.
The system may share coordination details such as identity when they are necessary.
The system may share relevant exposures when they are necessary.
The system may share dates when they are necessary.
The system may share current status when it is necessary.
The system shall support exceptions to the minimum-necessary information sharing rule.
The system shall ensure that exceptions are tightly controlled and documented.
The system shall allow additional details to be shared when a supervisor, privacy officer, or designated public health authority approves the disclosure.
The system shall record who approved the disclosure and why.
In read-only recovery mode, the system may provide limited printing or export if needed to keep operations going.
During recovery, the system shall keep the most sensitive notes hidden unless the user already has the required clearance.
During recovery, the system shall keep internal analysis hidden unless the user already has the required clearance.
During recovery, the system shall keep fields tied to restricted links or protected sources hidden unless the user already has the required clearance.
A jurisdiction with a different deployment sequence shall be allowed to proceed only if it can meet the minimum operational readiness criteria.
A jurisdiction with a hard dependency may need to go earlier than the normal pilot order or outside the normal pilot order.
A jurisdiction may require an earlier or non-standard go-live if it has a legacy interface that must be cut over on day one.
A jurisdiction may require an earlier or non-standard go-live if it has a migration that cannot be split safely.
A jurisdiction shall be allowed to go earlier or outside the normal pilot order only if testing, training, data validation, and support coverage are all in place.
A jurisdiction shall be delayed rather than forced live if the required conditions are not met.
Legacy outbreak cases should be fully converted if that can be done without losing important detail.
Legacy outbreak cases should not be reduced to a bare minimum if people still rely on them.
The system shall provide public health teams with a single place to manage an outbreak from first report through investigation and response.
The system shall help investigators identify related people and events.
The system shall monitor what is happening over time.
The system shall support reporting and coordination.
The system shall keep sensitive health information protected.
The system shall enable public health teams to move fast enough to contain a threat without losing track of critical details or exposing information to the wrong people.
The system shall allow users to capture case information.
The system shall allow users to capture contact information.
The system shall improve data quality.
The system shall support disease investigators as a main user group.
The system shall support epidemiologists as a main user group.
The system shall support lab staff or partners who provide specimen-related information.
The system shall support local public health teams with limited access for coordination in some situations.
Different groups shall have different access levels.
Investigators shall drive case work.
Lab and partner users may send results or supporting details that investigators need to reconcile.
The system shall support handoffs.
The system shall support task tracking.
The system shall support review workflows.
The system shall support more than data entry.
The system shall provide audit trails.
The system shall enforce permissions so users can collaborate without overwriting each other’s work.
The system shall use the field terms that investigators and other users already use, rather than inventing new labels.
The system shall tolerate connectivity interruptions in public health settings.
The system shall provide simple, guided screens for field staff and other less technical users.
The system shall support collaboration across multiple agencies and jurisdictions.
The system shall connect with lab reporting systems.
The system shall support one-way integrations for some feeds and two-way integrations where edits or status changes need to flow back.
The system shall not create duplicate work for users.
If an import fails, the system should show users a clear message explaining what went wrong.
For duplicates or incomplete data, the system should flag the issue and allow a trained user to review and resolve it.
For less technical users, the system should provide simple and actionable feedback.
For less technical users, the system should provide a "fix later" queue when a problem cannot be resolved immediately.
For more advanced users, the system should provide error details.
For more advanced users, the system should provide logs.
For more advanced users, the system should allow retrying the sync without starting over.
The system shall catch obvious validation problems immediately during data entry.
The system shall show users a clear message when the system is unavailable or an action could not be completed due to a system outage or unexpected error.
The system shall help users recover without confusion.
The system shall support configurable definitions or clearly defined value sets and metadata so users can see how a term was applied in a record.
For data sharing and access control, the system shall enforce the local rules of the owning agency before applying any sharing restrictions.
The system shall tie role-based access control to user job titles, jurisdiction, case ownership, and the sensitivity of the data being exchanged.
The system shall have clear required fields and standard definitions for each key entity.
The system shall use consistent identifiers and matching rules so the same person, specimen, or event can be recognized even if entered more than once.
The system shall provide a way to merge records when staff confirm they refer to the same entity.
If definitions differ by jurisdiction, the system shall keep a common core structure so reports and sharing stay consistent across agencies.
The system shall treat differences in term meaning across agencies or events as normal rather than exceptional.
The system shall support collaboration without flattening important nuance.
For data sharing, the system shall let the owning jurisdiction decide what data can be exposed and to whom.
The system shall combine role-based access with case-level permissions.
Users with the same role may still see different data based on agency, investigation assignment, or clearance.
The system shall allow administrators to configure local business rules, value sets, and status definitions without changing the core application.
The system shall support jurisdiction-specific alignment of configured rules to local policy.
The system shall provide metadata so users know which meaning applies to a record.
The system shall make differences between local rules and the viewer's own local rules obvious when a user reviews a record from another agency.
The system shall comply with public health privacy and security requirements such as HIPAA where applicable.
The system shall comply with state or local statutes that govern disease reporting and data sharing.
The system shall enable records to move between systems without losing meaning.
The system shall enforce very tight access controls on sensitive fields.
The system shall respect the legal authority under which data was collected when sharing data.
The system shall display the governing rule directly on the record rather than hiding it in administration screens.
The system shall indicate whether a field uses a federal standard, state rule, or local definition.
The system shall provide metadata for a record that includes any sharing restriction or legal basis attached to the record.
The user interface shall show prominent warnings when a record comes from another jurisdiction.
When a user edits something that has a local meaning, the system shall show the accepted definition.
When a user edits something that has a local meaning, the system shall prevent accidental overwriting of the source meaning unless the user has permission to do so.
The system shall automatically enforce jurisdiction ownership so records cannot be shared outside permitted agencies unless an authorized user approves the sharing under the correct policy.
The system shall apply the most restrictive rule set when local, state, and federal sharing requirements conflict.
The system shall override normal sharing when a case is subject to quarantine, embargo, or legal-hold conditions until the restriction is lifted.
The system shall be phased in because different agencies will not be ready at the same time.
The system shall account for a significant training burden during rollout.
The system implementation shall accommodate limited staff time for configuration and data migration.
The system shall be coordinated with existing state and local systems to avoid disrupting active outbreak operations.
The rollout shall allow enough time for testing with real public health users before wider deployment.
Releases shall be controlled rather than constant.
Feature updates shall be deployed on a monthly or quarterly cadence.
Before a release goes live in a new agency, configuration sign-off shall be obtained.
Before a release goes live in a new agency, security review shall be completed.
Changes that affect data definitions or sharing rules shall be approved by the relevant jurisdiction owner.
The system shall meet standard accessibility expectations.
The system shall be compatible with screen readers.
The system shall support full keyboard navigation.
The system shall provide good color contrast.
The system shall provide captions or text alternatives for media used by the system.
The system shall present forms and alerts in a simple manner.
The system shall provide error messages that clearly explain what went wrong and how to fix it.
The system shall support adjustable text size.
The system shall not rely only on color for critical tasks.
The system shall not rely only on drag-and-drop interactions for critical tasks.
During a major outbreak, the system shall remain responsive under heavy concurrent use.
The system shall support quick execution of common actions such as opening a record, saving a form, and running a routine search so that users are not waiting and retrying.
The system shall degrade gracefully under load.
When under load, the system shall keep essential functions available even if advanced reports or analytics slow down.
If the system has capacity limits, it shall make those limits visible and predictable rather than failing silently or losing work.
The system shall scale in both user count and data volume without requiring redesign as an outbreak grows.
The system shall ensure that core transaction functions and search handle growth well.
The system shall allow reporting and analytics to scale separately so they do not slow down day-to-day case work.
The system shall support multi-agency expansion through configuration.
The system shall not require custom code for multi-agency expansion.
The system shall allow archiving older events or partitioning data by jurisdiction or event.
The system shall allow authorized users to access data they are permitted to see without noticeable performance loss, even when data is archived or partitioned.
The system shall prioritize core operational actions such as viewing, creating, and updating cases, contacts, and exposures when load is high.
The system shall place nonessential functions such as large ad hoc analytics and bulk exports into a lower-priority queue when load is high.
If a request must be delayed, the system shall immediately tell the user that the request is pending and provide a realistic expectation for completion.
For capacity limits or slowdowns, the system shall show clear plain-language messages at the user's working location.
The system shall not hide capacity-limit or slowdown messages in logs or generic error pages.
The system shall preserve entered data so users do not lose work.
The system shall display visible indicators when a task takes longer than normal.
The system shall provide a spinner or progress bar for saves, searches, and report generation.
The system shall display a clear banner or status message when the platform is in a degraded mode.
The system shall avoid repeated pop-ups.
The system shall prioritize direct case management tasks over other work when under heavy strain.
The system shall defer or throttle large exports when the system is under strain.
The system shall defer or throttle complex cross-jurisdiction reports when the system is under strain.
The system shall defer or throttle bulk analytics when the system is under strain.
The system shall provide the busy notice before the user submits a heavy request when possible.
The system shall update the progress indicator or queued-request message if the task is still moving or delayed.
